entry: American actress. Born in Manhattan to actress [[Tippi Hedren]], she was raised mainly in Los Angeles. She appeared opposite [[Gene Hackman]] in *Night Moves* (1975) and was nominated for the Academy Award for Best Actress for *Working Girl* (1988), which also won her a Golden Globe. Her other films include *Body Double* (1984), directed by [[Brian De Palma]], and *Lolita* (1997). She was married to [[Antonio Banderas]], her co-star in *Autómata* (2014). She has discussed a 2009 diagnosis of [[Skin cancer]].

Family of biomolecules organized as oligomers or polymers, forming the pigments of many organisms. Melanin is produced by melanocytes in a process called melanogenesis, in which the [[Amino acid]] tyrosine is oxidized and then polymerized. There are five basic types: eumelanin, pheomelanin, neuromelanin, allomelanin and pyomelanin. Eumelanin is more abundant in tissues requiring photoprotection, such as the epidermis, and can dissipate over 99.9% of absorbed [[Ultraviolet|UV]] radiation. In human skin, melanogenesis is initiated by UV exposure, which is associated with increased risk of [[Melanoma]]. Pheomelanin is largely responsible for the red or yellow tint of some skin and hair. Neuromelanin, found in the brain, has been studied for possible treatment of neurodegenerative disorders such as Parkinson's.

Skin cancer arising from [[Melanin|melanin]]-producing cells called melanocytes. It typically occurs in the skin but may rarely occur in the mouth, intestines or eye. The primary cause is [[Ultraviolet|ultraviolet]] light exposure in people with low levels of skin pigment; risk is higher for those with many moles, a family history, or poor immune function. About 30% of melanomas develop from moles. Diagnosis is by [[Biopsy]]. Treatment is typically surgical removal, with lymph node testing for larger cancers. Immunotherapy, radiation or [[Chemotherapy]] may improve survival once the disease has spread. Five-year survival rates in the United States are 100% for localized disease, 76% when the disease has spread to lymph nodes, and 35% for distant spread. Melanoma is the most dangerous type of skin cancer; worldwide cases are expected to rise from 331,722 in 2022 to 510,000 in 2040, although mortality is decreasing.

Capital and most populous city of the Australian state of [[Victoria (state)|Victoria]] (pop., June 2025: 5,435,000). It is the second-most populous city in [[Australia]]. Founded in 1835 by free settlers from Van Diemen's Land (modern-day [[Tasmania]]), it was named after the British prime minister William Lamb, 2nd Viscount Melbourne. [[Queen Victoria]] declared it a city in 1847. The city boomed during the 1850s [[Gold rush]] and became capital of the Colony of Victoria in 1851. After federation in 1901 it was the interim seat of government until [[Canberra]] became the permanent capital in 1927. Melbourne is a leading financial center in the Asia-Pacific region. Landmarks include the Melbourne Cricket Ground and the National Gallery of Victoria. The city gave rise to [[Australian rules football]], hosts the Australian Open [[Grand Slam (tennis)|Grand Slam]] tennis tournament, and hosted the 1956 Summer Olympics. Melbourne Airport is the second-busiest airport in Australia.

Biblical king of Salem and [[Priest]] of El Elyon ("God Most High"). He appears in Genesis 14:18–20, where he brings out bread and wine and blesses [[Abraham]], and in Psalm 110:4. In the [[New Testament]], the Epistle to the Hebrews calls [[Jesus]] a "high priest forever in the order of Melchizedek". Joseph Blenkinsopp has suggested that the Genesis story is an informal insertion, possibly made to validate the priesthood and titles of the Second Temple. The name is usually rendered "king of righteousness", though it has been conjectured that its suffix refers to a [[Canaan|Canaanite]] deity worshipped in Jerusalem.

Linear succession of musical tones that the listener perceives as a single entity. In its most literal sense a melody combines pitch and [[Rhythm]], while more figuratively it can include tonal color. It is the foreground to a background accompaniment, and is often built from motifs repeated in various forms. Melodies are described by their melodic motion, pitch range, tension and release, and cadence. In [[Classical music]], composers often introduce an initial melody or theme and then create variations, and several melodic layers may form polyphony, as in a [[Fugue]]. [[Jazz]] musicians use the "lead" or "head" as the starting point for improvisation. [[Rock music]] and folk styles tend to pick one or two melodies and stick with them. [[Indian classical music]] relies more on melody and rhythm than on [[Harmony]], while Balinese [[Gamelan]] often plays complicated variations of a single melody simultaneously.

Phase transition of a [[Solid]] to a [[Liquid]]. It occurs when the [[Internal energy]] of the solid increases, typically through heat or pressure, raising its temperature to the melting point. At that point the ordering of ions or [[Molecule|molecules]] breaks down. Melting is a first-order phase transition: at the melting point the change in Gibbs free energy is zero, while enthalpy and entropy change. Substances in the molten state generally have reduced [[Viscosity]] as temperature rises; elemental sulfur is an exception, because its viscosity increases between 130 °C and 190 °C due to polymerization. Water on a very clean glass surface can supercool several degrees below its freezing point. Low-temperature [[Helium-3]] has a negative enthalpy of fusion below 0.3 K, so heat must be removed to melt it.

Cultural idea, behavior or style transmitted by imitation from person to person within a [[Culture]]. Supporters regard memes as cultural analogues to [[Gene|genes]], in that they self-replicate, [[Mutation|mutate]] and respond to selective pressures. Proponents suggest memes evolve by [[Natural selection]]. The word was coined by [[Richard Dawkins]] in *The Selfish Gene* (1976), shortened from *mimeme* on the model of *gene*. In popular usage a meme is often an [[Internet meme]], typically an image remixed and circulated online. Memetics, a field of study that arose in the 1990s, has faced criticism that academic study cannot examine memes empirically.

Artistic symbol or trope reminding viewers of the inevitability of [[Death]]. The [[Latin]] phrase means "remember [that you have] to die". Its roots lie in [[Classical antiquity]] and [[Christianity]], and it appeared in funerary art and architecture from the medieval period onward. The most common motif is a skull, often with bones; coffins, hourglasses and wilting flowers also signify impermanence. Standalone genres include the *vanitas* and *danse macabre*. In Roman triumphs, a companion stood behind the general and reminded him of his mortality. [[Tertullian]] alone records the full phrase, "Respice post te! Hominem te memento!" ("Look behind you! Remember that you are a man!").

Electronic data storage device using flash memory to hold digital information. Memory cards are used in digital cameras, action cameras, drones, e-readers, handheld game consoles and some [[Smartphone|smartphones]], where a card in a socket adds storage without protruding USB flash drives. Common types include [[SD card|SD cards]] (including microSD), [[Sony]]'s Memory Stick and CompactFlash; as of 2024 SD cards are the most common. Flash memory was invented by Fujio Masuoka at Toshiba in 1980 and commercialized in 1987. In the 1980s memory cards were developed as an alternative to [[Floppy disk|floppy disk]] drives, which used less power and occupied less space in laptops. The SD card was announced in 2000 as a single format for several kinds of devices. Early memory cards were expensive, costing US$3 per megabyte of capacity in 2001.

Ancient capital of [[Ancient Egypt|Egypt]] near the present-day village of Mit Rahina, Giza Governorate. According to legend it was founded by King Menes. It was the capital during the Early Dynastic Period and the Old Kingdom, and its principal port, Peru-nefer, distributed food and merchandise throughout the kingdom. Its great temple, Hut-ka-Ptah, honored Ptah, patron of craftsmen; the name is believed to be the etymological origin of the English name "Egypt". Memphis and its necropolis, including the [[Giza|Pyramids of Giza]] fields, are a [[World Heritage Site]] and an open-air museum. Its importance declined after the rise of coastal [[Alexandria]] in late antiquity. By the Middle Ages nearby [[Cairo]] had become a major political and economic center.

City on the [[Mississippi River]] in [[Tennessee]] (pop., 2020: 633,104), seat of Shelby County. Founded in 1819 by [[Andrew Jackson]], John Overton and James Winchester, it grew on river traffic and cotton before the [[American Civil War]]. FedEx, the largest employer, has its global air hub at Memphis International Airport. The city is known for [[Blues]], [[Soul music]], [[Rock and roll]] and hip-hop. The 1968 Memphis Sanitation Strike led to the assassination of [[Martin Luther King Jr.]] at the Lorraine Motel, now the National Civil Rights Museum.

Indo-Greek king (reigned c. 165/155–130 BC) of northwestern [[Indian subcontinent]] and [[Central Asia]]. He may first have been a prince or king of [[Bactria]]. After conquering the [[Punjab]], as far as Taxila and Sagala, he established an empire from the Kabul River to the Ravi River. The Greek geographer Strabo wrote that he "conquered more tribes than [[Alexander the Great]]" in India. Large numbers of his coins have been found. Menander was a patron of [[Buddhism]], and his conversations with the Buddhist sage Nagasena are recorded in the *Milinda Panha* ("The Questions of King Milinda"). He was succeeded by his wife Agathoclea, who ruled as regent for his son Strato I. According to [[Plutarch]], he died on campaign and his remains were divided among cities for enshrinement in monuments.

Chinese Confucian philosopher, often called the Second Sage. A fourth-generation disciple of [[Confucius]], he is said to have been a pupil of Zisi, Confucius's grandson. Born Meng Ke in the state of Zou, he traveled among the states of the [[Warring States period]], offering counsel to rulers. Conversations with these rulers form the basis of the *Mencius*, later canonized as a Confucian classic. He held that human nature is righteous and humane, and that rulers derive legitimacy from the [[Mandate of Heaven]], contingent on the welfare of the people. His view opposed that of [[Xunzi (philosopher)|Xunzi]], who held that human nature is evil. The idiom "Mencius's mother moves three times" refers to choosing a proper environment for raising children.

Type of biological inheritance following the principles proposed by [[Gregor Mendel]] in 1865 and 1866. Its defining feature is a heavy association with a single [[Gene]]. Mendel's principles were rediscovered in 1900 by Hugo de Vries, Carl Correns and Erich von Tschermak. In 1915 Thomas Hunt Morgan integrated them with the chromosome theory of inheritance, forming the core of classical [[Genetics]]. [[Ronald Fisher]] combined them with [[Natural selection]] in *The Genetical Theory of Natural Selection* (1930), putting evolution on a mathematical footing. Between 1856 and 1863 Mendel tested some 28,000 [[Pea]] plants. Mendelian principles underpin the study of monogenic disorders, such as Huntington's disease and cystic fibrosis.

Emperor of Ethiopia from 1889 to 1913 and king of Shewa from 1866 to 1889. A member of the Solomonic dynasty, he expanded the [[Ethiopian Empire]] to its greatest historical extent. Born Sahle Maryam in Ankober, he was named Menelik after the legendary son of [[Solomon]] and the [[Queen of Sheba]]. After the death of [[Yohannes IV]] at the Battle of Metemma in 1889, he was crowned emperor at Mount Entoto. He signed the Treaty of Wuchale with [[Italy]] in 1889 but later rejected it. At the Battle of Adwa on 1 March 1896, his army of over 100,000 defeated the Italian invasion, securing Ethiopia's independence. He made [[Addis Ababa]] the new capital and initiated the Addis Ababa–Djibouti Railway. Critics among incorporated ethnic groups accused him of forced assimilation and land expropriation, while he is widely regarded as the founder of modern Ethiopia.

Acute or chronic [[Inflammation]] of the protective membranes covering the [[Brain]] and [[Spinal cord]]. Common symptoms are fever, intense headache, vomiting and neck stiffness; young children may show only irritability or poor feeding. Causes include viruses, bacteria, fungi and parasites, as well as non-infectious causes such as cancer. It is a medical emergency, and a [[Lumbar puncture]] can diagnose it. Treatment includes prompt [[Antibiotic|antibiotics]], sometimes antiviral drugs, and corticosteroids to prevent complications. Long-term consequences can include deafness, epilepsy, hydrocephalus or cognitive deficits. Some forms are preventable by [[Vaccination]]. In 2019 about 7.7 million people were diagnosed worldwide and 236,000 died, down from 433,000 deaths in 1990.

Anabaptist Christian communities tracing their roots to the Radical [[Reformation]]. The name derives from the Frisian cleric Menno Simons, whose writings formalized the teachings of earlier Swiss Anabaptists. The Dordrecht Confession of Faith (1632) affirmed the [[Baptism|baptism]] of believers only, nonresistance and other principles. Mennonites are known as a historic peace church because of their commitment to pacifism. Practice ranges from Old Order groups that avoid some modern technology to mainline Mennonites indistinguishable in dress from the general population. Mennonites live in 87 countries; the largest populations are in Canada, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Ethiopia, India and the United States.

Permanent end of menstrual periods, marking the close of the reproductive phase in female humans. Medically, menopause is defined as having occurred after a year without menstrual bleeding. The transition has three stages: perimenopause, menopause and postmenopause. Natural menopause typically occurs between the ages of 45 and 55, as production of [[Estrogen]] and progesterone declines. Surgical removal of both ovaries also causes menopause, and ovarian failure before age 40 is termed premature ovarian insufficiency. Symptoms include hot flashes, night sweats, vaginal dryness and mood changes. Physical consequences include bone loss and increased risk of [[Osteoporosis]] and [[Cardiovascular disease]]. Menopausal hormone therapy is effective for many symptoms and for preventing bone loss. Non-hormonal options for hot flashes include cognitive-behavioral therapy and [[Gabapentin]].

Recurring series of hormonal and structural changes in the [[Female reproductive system]]. Its ovarian cycle controls the release of [[Egg cell|eggs]] and the cyclic release of [[Estrogen|estrogen]] and progesterone, while its uterine cycle prepares the lining of the [[Uterus]] to receive an [[Embryo]]. Cycles usually last 21 to 35 days, with a median of 28 days. Menarche usually occurs around age 12, and cycles continue for about 30–45 years until [[Menopause]]. Around day 14 an egg is usually released. Falling progesterone triggers [[Menstruation]], the shedding of the lining, which signals that [[Pregnancy]] has not occurred. Hormonal birth control can modify the cycle.

Regular discharge of blood and mucosal tissue from the uterine lining through the [[Vagina]], also called a period. Falling progesterone triggers it, and it signals that [[Pregnancy]] has not occurred. The first period, menarche, usually begins during [[Puberty]] between ages 11 and 13. Bleeding typically lasts two to seven days. Periods stop during pregnancy and typically do not resume in the first months of [[Breastfeeding]], ending permanently at [[Menopause]]. Premenstrual syndrome affects 20 to 30% of women, with 3 to 8% experiencing severe symptoms. During their periods, 38% of women reported being unable to perform all regular daily activities.

Hypothetical internal cognitive symbol representing external reality or its abstractions, studied in [[Philosophy of mind]] and [[Cognitive psychology]]. Mental representations allow people to imagine things never experienced or that do not exist. The representational theory of mind, in which representations act as intermediaries between observer and world, can be traced to [[Thomas Hobbes]] and was a dominant theme of [[Empiricism|classical empiricism]]. Modern proponents such as Jerry Fodor and Steven Pinker describe an internal language of thought, or mentalese, with [[Syntax]] and [[Semantics]] similar to natural languages. Stephen Kosslyn proposes that images help solve certain problems. How the brain interprets and stores representational content remains debated.

Genus of flowering plants in the mint family, [[Lamiaceae]], with an estimated 18 to 24 species. It is a member of the tribe Mentheae in the subfamily Nepetoideae. Mints are almost exclusively perennial herbs with square, branched stems and spreading stolons, and some are considered invasive. Their leaves are arranged in opposite pairs, and their white to purple flowers form false whorls. Hybridization occurs naturally where species' ranges overlap, producing many [[Hybrid (biology)|hybrids]] and [[Cultivar|cultivars]]. The genus grows best in wet environments and moist soils. Peppermint, *Mentha* × *piperita*, is a hybrid of *M. aquatica* and *M. spicata*. Mint essential oils are rich in [[Menthol]].

Monoterpenoid organic compound found naturally in the oils of [[Mentha|mint]]-family plants such as peppermint and corn mint. It is a white or clear waxy crystalline solid. Menthol produces a cooling sensation when inhaled, eaten or applied to the skin, and has local anesthetic and counterirritant qualities. It is widely used to relieve minor throat irritation and as a flavoring. The cooling effect comes from chemical activation of cold-sensitive TRPM8 receptors. Its anesthetic properties resemble those of [[Propofol]], though it is less potent.

Organomercuric disodium [[Salt (chemistry)|salt]] used as a topical antiseptic for minor cuts and scrapes and as a biological [[Dye]]. Marketed as Mercurochrome, its antiseptic qualities were discovered in 1918 by Hugh H. Young at Johns Hopkins Hospital. In 1998 the U.S. Food and Drug Administration reclassified it from "generally recognized as safe" to "untested", owing to a lack of recent studies. Because of its [[Mercury (element)|mercury]] content, it is no longer sold in the [[United States]]. It is synthesized by combining dibromofluorescein with mercuric acetate and [[Sodium hydroxide]]. Because of its anionic character, it is incompatible with acids, most [[Alkaloid]] salts and local anesthetics.
